newsitem.title: UK: THE PROTEUS COLUMN - SPACE INSURANCE CONFERENCE.
newsitem.headline: THE PROTEUS COLUMN - SPACE INSURANCE CONFERENCE.

text.p: THE PROTEUS COLUMN
On Thursday delegates gather for the biennial space insurance conference hosted by Italian insurer Generali in Venice, to discuss the insurance implications of commercial developments in space.

They will be holding their breath that Western Europe's 95th Ariane rocket takes off without hitch tomorrow from French Guiana carrying two satellites to service Asia. For, as one leading underwriter told Proteus, there is an unfortunate tradition that a major accident takes place before or during the conference.
But in fact it is the continued improvement in space technology which will affect delegates' business, more than its failures.

The Global space market capacity appears to have stabilised at around USD600 million per launch, although brokers say this will edge upward during the year as more underwriters come in attracted by the high earnings potential in this sector.

Despite some highly publicised losses, like the Ariane 5 crash last year, underwriters have enjoyed profits in seven of the last ten years. In two of the loss years, 1988 and 1990, the loss was marginal. The USD175 million loss in 1994 was the only significant disappointment in the period.
The sector is vulnerable because it is marked by a limited spread of business, high-value risks, and leading-edge technology that is relatively untested and can require costly refinement.
For this reason, space underwriters are often asked to venture out into the unknown to support innovative but unproven risks, and they are understandably reluctant to do so at knock-down prices.

According to a report by Johnson & Higgins, launch failure rates currently run just below 20% of insured values. Until confidence in these risk increases, space will remain a volatile sector in terms of pricing and market capacity.

However as technology advances, space risks will almost certainly become more reliable and the number of launches more frequent. Profitability should therefore be sustained on higher volumes and lower margins. As with every insurance cycle, this will in turn lead to more competition and pressure on rates.

New space vehicles usually command higher rates, but the growing trend towards satellite package placements, where as many as 10 satellites are insured under one policy, is likely to continue as it offers discount rates to buyers and spreads underwriters risks.

At this week's conference someone will no doubt again bring up the issue of whether the space sector should move to a vertical market. Currently all participants get the same terms and conditions, rather than different parts of the insurance programme being placed with different insurers at different prices as happens in aviation.
As usual there will be resistance, but as pressure for market share increases, there is more chance that vertical marketing - which promotes price competition - will be accepted.
